name: Appeal to Probability
definition: Taking something for granted because it would probably be the case, or might possibly be the case.
pattern: X would probably happen; therefore X is true/assumed.
example_textbook: Since most cars in this lot are red, the car that was stolen was probably red.
example_conversational: I mean, statistically most break-ins happen at night, so it definitely happened at night.

name: Argument from Fallacy
definition: Assuming that if a particular argument for a conclusion is fallacious, the conclusion itself must be false.
pattern: Argument for X is fallacious; therefore X is false.
example_textbook: Your argument for God's existence was a logical fallacy, so God must not exist.
example_conversational: That study you cited had a cherry-picking problem, so vaccines obviously don't work.

name: Base Rate Fallacy
definition: Making a probability judgment based on conditional probabilities without accounting for prior (base rate) probabilities.
pattern: P(evidence|hypothesis) is high; therefore P(hypothesis|evidence) is high, ignoring base rates.
example_textbook: The test is 99% accurate, so if you tested positive for the rare disease, you almost certainly have it.
example_conversational: He failed the lie detector, so he's basically guilty — those things are like 90% accurate.

name: Conjunction Fallacy
definition: Assuming that an outcome satisfying multiple conditions simultaneously is more probable than an outcome satisfying just one of them.
pattern: P(A and B) judged > P(A).
example_textbook: Linda is a feminist and a bank teller is judged more likely than Linda is a bank teller.
example_conversational: It's more likely he's a quiet, brilliant programmer who also plays chess than just that he's a programmer.

name: Masked-Man Fallacy
definition: Substituting identical designators in a true statement can lead to a false one, due to differing epistemic contexts.
pattern: A=B is true; I know A; therefore I know B (fails if A=B is not known).
example_textbook: I know who my best friend is. The masked man is my best friend (unknown to me). Therefore I know who the masked man is.
example_conversational: You said you trust the CEO. The CEO is the leaker. So you trust the leaker — but you didn't know that.

name: Affirming a Disjunct
definition: Concluding that one disjunct must be false because the other disjunct is true, in an inclusive 'or' statement.
pattern: A or B; A; therefore not B.
example_textbook: It's either raining or cloudy. It's raining. Therefore it's not cloudy.
example_conversational: She's either tired or annoyed. She's clearly tired, so she can't be annoyed too.

name: Affirming the Consequent
definition: Claiming the antecedent of a conditional is true because the consequent is true.
pattern: If A, then B; B; therefore A.
example_textbook: If it rains, the ground is wet. The ground is wet. Therefore it rained.
example_conversational: If he's lying, he'd avoid eye contact. He's avoiding eye contact, so he must be lying.

name: Denying the Antecedent
definition: Claiming the consequent of a conditional is false because the antecedent is false.
pattern: If A, then B; not A; therefore not B.
example_textbook: If you study, you'll pass. You didn't study. Therefore you won't pass.
example_conversational: If we cut taxes, the economy grows. We're not cutting taxes, so the economy won't grow.

name: Existential Fallacy
definition: A syllogism with a universal premise but a particular conclusion, which illegitimately assumes existence.
pattern: All A are B; therefore some A exist that are B.
example_textbook: All trespassers will be prosecuted; therefore some trespassers exist.
example_conversational: All unicorns have horns, so there must be some unicorns out there with horns.

name: Affirmative Conclusion from a Negative Premise
definition: A categorical syllogism reaches a positive conclusion despite having at least one negative premise.
pattern: No A are B; some C are A; therefore some C are B.
example_textbook: No fish are mammals. Some pets are fish. Therefore some pets are mammals.
example_conversational: None of the interns finished early, and some interns are juniors, so some juniors finished early.

name: Fallacy of Exclusive Premises
definition: An invalid categorical syllogism in which both premises are negative.
pattern: No A are B; no B are C; therefore (invalid conclusion about A and C).
example_textbook: No cats are dogs. No dogs are birds. Therefore no cats are birds (invalid form, even if true).
example_conversational: No managers signed off, and no executives reviewed it, so clearly nobody approved it.

name: Fallacy of Four Terms
definition: A categorical syllogism that improperly contains four distinct terms instead of three.
pattern: All A are B; all C are D; therefore all A are D.
example_textbook: All humans are mortal. All Greeks are rational. Therefore all humans are rational.
example_conversational: Engineers are logical. Doctors are caring. So engineers must be caring.

name: Illicit Major
definition: A categorical syllogism invalid because its major term is undistributed in the major premise but distributed in the conclusion.
pattern: All A are B; no C are A; therefore no C are B.
example_textbook: All dogs are mammals. No cats are dogs. Therefore no cats are mammals.
example_conversational: All our top performers are remote. None of the new hires are remote. So none of the new hires are top performers.

name: Illicit Minor
definition: A categorical syllogism invalid because its minor term is undistributed in the minor premise but distributed in the conclusion.
pattern: All A are B; all A are C; therefore all C are B.
example_textbook: All squares are rectangles. All squares are quadrilaterals. Therefore all quadrilaterals are rectangles.
example_conversational: All our best clients pay on time. All our best clients are local. So all local clients pay on time.

name: Negative Conclusion from Affirmative Premises
definition: A categorical syllogism with a negative conclusion despite having only affirmative premises.
pattern: All A are B; all B are C; therefore some C are not A.
example_textbook: All roses are flowers. All flowers are plants. Therefore some plants are not roses (drawn as a negative when premises were affirmative).
example_conversational: All our products are tested, and all tested items are logged, so some logged items aren't our products.

name: Fallacy of the Undistributed Middle
definition: The middle term in a categorical syllogism is never distributed, making the syllogism invalid.
pattern: All A are B; all C are B; therefore all A are C.
example_textbook: All dogs are animals. All cats are animals. Therefore all dogs are cats.
example_conversational: All our competitors raised prices, and we raised prices too, so we must be acting like our competitors.

name: Modal Fallacy
definition: Confusing what is necessary for an outcome with what is sufficient for it.
pattern: X is necessary for Y; therefore X is sufficient for Y (or vice versa).
example_textbook: Oxygen is necessary for fire, so wherever there is oxygen there must be fire.
example_conversational: You need funding to launch a startup, so if you have funding, the startup will launch.

name: Modal Scope Fallacy
definition: Placing an unwarranted degree of necessity onto the conclusion that wasn't present in the premises.
pattern: Necessarily (if A, then B); A; therefore necessarily B.
example_textbook: It is necessarily true that if you're a bachelor, you're unmarried. You're a bachelor. Therefore you're necessarily unmarried (conflating logical necessity with the modal status of the conclusion).
example_conversational: If the data's accurate, the model must be right, and since the data could theoretically be accurate, the model has to be right.

name: Argument from Incredulity
definition: Concluding something is false because one cannot imagine it being true, or true because one cannot imagine it being false.
pattern: I cannot imagine how X could be true; therefore X is false.
example_textbook: I can't see how the universe could have just appeared from nothing, so something must have created it.
example_conversational: There's no way she figured that out on her own — I just can't picture it, so someone must've helped her.

name: Argument to Moderation
definition: Assuming that the compromise between two positions is always correct.
pattern: Position A; position B; therefore the truth is the midpoint between A and B.
example_textbook: Some say the earth is round, others say it's flat — the truth is probably that it's somewhat round.
example_conversational: You think we should fire him, I think we should give him a raise — let's just split the difference and keep his pay the same.

name: Continuum Fallacy
definition: Improperly rejecting a claim because it is vague or imprecise at the margins, despite being clear in central cases.
pattern: There's no precise cutoff between A and not-A; therefore the distinction between A and not-A doesn't exist.
example_textbook: There's no exact moment a person becomes 'old,' so the concept of old age is meaningless.
example_conversational: Nobody can say exactly when 'a lot of meetings' becomes 'too many meetings,' so you can't really say we have too many.

name: Suppressed Correlative
definition: Redefining a correlative term so that one of the alternatives becomes impossible.
pattern: Redefine X relative to Y such that not-X becomes unattainable by definition.
example_textbook: I'm not fat because I'm thinner than John.
example_conversational: I'm not really 'late' for things — I just show up whenever I show up, and that's when it starts for me.

name: Double Counting
definition: Counting events or occurrences more than once in probabilistic reasoning, inflating the apparent probability.
pattern: P(A) + P(A again under a different label) summed as if independent.
example_textbook: Counting the probability of rain on Saturday AND the probability of rain this weekend as separate, additive risks.
example_conversational: We've got the budget risk, the timeline risk, and the 'budget timeline' risk — that's three separate things to worry about.

name: Ecological Fallacy
definition: Inferring something about an individual based solely on aggregate statistics about the group they belong to.
pattern: Group G has average property P; individual X belongs to G; therefore X has property P.
example_textbook: This neighborhood has a high average income, so that person living there must be wealthy.
example_conversational: Engineers at this company tend to be introverted, so he's probably pretty quiet.

name: Equivocation
definition: Using a word with more than one meaning in an argument without clarifying which meaning is intended, in a way that misleads.
pattern: X is A (meaning 1); A implies B (meaning 2); therefore X is B.
example_textbook: A feather is light. What is light cannot be dark. Therefore a feather cannot be dark.
example_conversational: He said he's 'open' to feedback, so clearly he's an open book about everything in his life.

name: Ambiguous Middle Term
definition: A syllogism's middle term is used with two different meanings across the premises.
pattern: All A are B(meaning 1); all B(meaning 2) are C; therefore all A are C.
example_textbook: Power corrupts. Knowledge is power. Therefore knowledge corrupts.
example_conversational: Banks are secure. The data is in the cloud bank. Therefore the data is secure.

name: Motte-and-Bailey Fallacy
definition: Conflating an easily-defended modest position (the motte) with a more controversial one (the bailey), retreating to the former when challenged.
pattern: Assert controversial claim B; when challenged, defend only modest claim A as if it were B.
example_textbook: Claiming 'all cultures are equally valid' (bailey), but when challenged, retreating to 'we shouldn't judge other cultures unfairly' (motte).
example_conversational: He says 'the system is rigged against us,' but when pressed he just means 'sometimes things are unfair' — much easier to defend.

name: Fallacy of Accent
definition: Changing the meaning of a statement by shifting which word is emphasized, without making the shift explicit.
pattern: Statement S with stress on word W1 means X; restated with stress on W2, S now implies Y.
example_textbook: 'We should not speak ill of our friends' can imply it's fine to speak ill of others, depending on stress.
example_conversational: He said 'I didn't say she stole it' — emphasis on 'I' implies someone else said it, which he later used to deny the accusation entirely.

name: Persuasive Definition
definition: Presenting a biased or unusual definition of a term as though it were the standard, commonly accepted one.
pattern: Redefine term T with built-in evaluative spin; argue using T as if neutrally defined.
example_textbook: Defining 'freedom' as 'doing whatever benefits society' to argue that restricting individual choice is actually freedom.
example_conversational: He calls it 'just being direct,' but what he means by 'direct' is being rude without consequences.

name: Etymological Fallacy
definition: Assuming a word's original or historical meaning must govern or match its present-day usage.
pattern: Word W originally meant M; therefore W must still mean M today.
example_textbook: 'Decimate' originally meant 'reduce by a tenth,' so using it to mean 'destroy almost entirely' is wrong.
example_conversational: 'Awful' used to mean 'awe-inspiring,' so technically calling something awful should be a compliment.

name: Fallacy of Composition
definition: Assuming that something true of the parts of a whole must also be true of the whole itself.
pattern: Each part of X has property P; therefore X (the whole) has property P.
example_textbook: Every player on the team is excellent, so the team must be excellent.
example_conversational: Each line of the budget looks reasonable, so the whole budget must be reasonable.

name: Fallacy of Division
definition: Assuming that something true of a whole must also be true of its individual parts.
pattern: X (the whole) has property P; therefore each part of X has property P.
example_textbook: This company is highly profitable, so every department in it must be profitable.
example_conversational: Our team hit its targets this quarter, so everyone on the team must have hit their individual targets.

name: False Attribution
definition: Appealing to an irrelevant, unqualified, biased, or fabricated source to support an argument.
pattern: Source S (unreliable/irrelevant) says X; therefore X is true.
example_textbook: A blog with no credentials claims the new policy will fail, so it must be a bad policy.
example_conversational: My cousin's friend who works in tech says AI is definitely going to replace all jobs by next year.

name: Fallacy of Quoting Out of Context
definition: Selectively excerpting words from their original context in a way that distorts their intended meaning.
pattern: Quote fragment F from source S, omitting context C that reverses F's meaning.
example_textbook: Cutting 'I don't think this plan will fail' down to 'this plan will fail.'
example_conversational: He said 'I'm not saying it's impossible, but it's extremely unlikely' and they reported it as 'CEO admits it's impossible.'

name: False Authority
definition: Citing an expert of dubious or irrelevant credentials, or relying on a single opinion, to support a claim.
pattern: Person P (not a relevant expert) says X; therefore X is true.
example_textbook: A famous actor endorses a diet supplement as medically effective.
example_conversational: My personal trainer says this investment strategy is solid, so I'm going all in.

name: False Dilemma
definition: Presenting only two options as if they were the only possibilities when more exist.
pattern: Either A or B; not A; therefore B (when C, D, etc. are also possible).
example_textbook: You're either with us or against us.
example_conversational: Either we cut the whole team's budget or the project fails completely — those are our only options.

name: False Equivalence
definition: Describing two or more things as essentially equal when meaningful differences make them not comparable.
pattern: A and B share property P; therefore A and B are equivalent.
example_textbook: Both candidates have made misleading statements, so they're equally dishonest.
example_conversational: He was 5 minutes late once and she's been late every day this month, but you're treating it like the same problem.

name: Historian's Fallacy
definition: Assuming that decision-makers in the past had the same information available as those who later analyze their decisions.
pattern: We now know X; therefore the historical actor should have known X and acted accordingly.
example_textbook: Judging a 19th-century general for not anticipating a tactic that was only understood decades later.
example_conversational: Why didn't the team pivot earlier — it's so obvious now that the market was shifting.

name: Historical Fallacy
definition: Believing a result occurred only because a specific process was performed, when the process may be unrelated to the outcome.
pattern: Process P was performed; outcome O occurred; therefore P caused O.
example_textbook: We followed the exact same five-step ritual before our last win, so we must repeat it to win again.
example_conversational: We did the all-hands meeting right before the deal closed, so the meeting must be why it closed.

name: Homunculus Fallacy
definition: Explaining a concept by inserting a smaller, unexplained version of the same concept, without real explanatory progress.
pattern: X is explained by a smaller X-like agent inside the system, which itself goes unexplained.
example_textbook: Thoughts are produced by a little 'thinker' inside the brain who does the thinking.
example_conversational: The model 'understands' the prompt because there's an internal reasoning module that understands it.

name: Inflation of Conflict
definition: Arguing that because experts disagree on a point, no conclusion can be reached or the field itself is illegitimate.
pattern: Expert A and Expert B disagree on X; therefore X is unknowable / the field is bunk.
example_textbook: Nutritionists disagree about the ideal diet, so nutrition science is worthless.
example_conversational: Economists can't even agree on inflation forecasts, so the whole field is basically guesswork.

name: If-by-Whiskey
definition: Supporting both sides of an issue at once by using emotionally loaded, ambiguous language tailored to each audience.
pattern: If you mean X (negative framing), I oppose it; if you mean X (positive framing), I support it — said to please everyone.
example_textbook: A politician's classic 'if by whiskey' speech supporting and opposing alcohol depending on the listener's leaning.
example_conversational: If 'flexible hours' means people slacking off, I'm against it; if it means trusting professionals, I'm all for it — so vote however you want.

name: Incomplete Comparison
definition: Making a comparison without providing enough information to evaluate it meaningfully.
pattern: X is better/more than Y (comparison basis unspecified or missing).
example_textbook: This new phone is 50% faster!
example_conversational: Our new plan saves you more money — without saying more than what, or under what conditions.

name: Kettle Logic
definition: Using multiple jointly inconsistent arguments to defend the same position.
pattern: Defend X using argument A; also defend X using argument B, where A and B contradict each other.
example_textbook: I never borrowed your kettle. It was already broken when I borrowed it. Also, I returned it in perfect condition.
example_conversational: I wasn't even at the meeting, and besides, what I said there was taken out of context, and anyway everyone agreed with me.

name: Ludic Fallacy
definition: Failing to account for unknown unknowns and real-world randomness when applying simplified probabilistic models.
pattern: Model M assigns probability P to event E (ignoring unmodeled real-world risk factors).
example_textbook: A risk model based on historical data fails to predict a market crash caused by an unprecedented event.
example_conversational: Our simulation says there's only a 1% chance of failure, so we're basically guaranteed to be fine.

name: Lump of Labour Fallacy
definition: The misconception that there is a fixed amount of work in an economy, so automation or immigration necessarily reduces jobs for others.
pattern: Total work is fixed; if group A does work W, group B has less work available.
example_textbook: Immigrants are taking jobs that would otherwise go to native workers.
example_conversational: If we automate this process, that's just fewer jobs for people, period.

name: McNamara Fallacy
definition: Making decisions based only on quantitative measures, discounting qualitative factors that resist measurement.
pattern: Metric M is high/low; therefore the decision is correct, ignoring unmeasured qualitative factors.
example_textbook: Judging the success of a war solely by body counts, ignoring strategic and humanitarian context.
example_conversational: Her ticket-closing numbers are the highest on the team, so she's clearly our best support rep.

name: Mind Projection Fallacy
definition: Assuming a statement about an object describes an inherent property of the object rather than a feature of one's own perception.
pattern: I perceive X as P; therefore X inherently has property P.
example_textbook: Calling a quantum particle's state 'uncertain' as if uncertainty is a property of the particle rather than of our knowledge.
example_conversational: This task feels impossible, so it must actually be impossible.

name: Moving the Goalposts
definition: Dismissing evidence presented for a claim and demanding additional, often greater, evidence instead.
pattern: Provide evidence E for claim C; responder demands evidence E2 > E, repeatedly.
example_textbook: Show me one peer-reviewed study. [Shown one.] Well, now show me ten, from different countries, over twenty years.
example_conversational: I showed you the receipts. Okay, now show me the bank statement too. And the email confirming it. And...

name: Nirvana Fallacy
definition: Rejecting a solution because it is not perfect, ignoring that it may still be a meaningful improvement.
pattern: Solution S does not fully solve problem P; therefore S should be rejected.
example_textbook: Seatbelts don't prevent all car deaths, so there's no point in requiring them.
example_conversational: This new process won't eliminate every bug, so why bother changing anything?

name: Package Deal Fallacy
definition: Treating essentially dissimilar concepts as though they necessarily go together.
pattern: X and Y are typically grouped together; therefore accepting X requires accepting Y.
example_textbook: If you support free markets, you must also oppose all forms of regulation.
example_conversational: If you care about the environment, you have to support this specific policy too.

name: Proof by Assertion
definition: Repeating a claim over and over, regardless of contradiction, as if repetition establishes truth.
pattern: X (restated repeatedly, without new support).
example_textbook: This product is the best — and again, it's simply the best, hands down the best.
example_conversational: I keep telling you, this plan will work. It will work. I'm telling you, it'll work.

name: Prosecutor's Fallacy
definition: Confusing the low probability of a false match with a low probability that a given match is false, ignoring the number of opportunities for a false match.
pattern: P(evidence|innocent) is low; therefore P(innocent|evidence) is low (ignoring population size/search space).
example_textbook: The DNA match has a 1-in-a-million error rate, so this match must be correct — ignoring that millions of people were searched.
example_conversational: The algorithm flagged his transaction as fraud, and it's 99.9% accurate, so he's basically guilty.

name: Proving Too Much
definition: An argument's logic, if valid, would also prove an absurd or clearly false additional conclusion.
pattern: Argument for X also implies absurd Y by the same logic; therefore the argument is flawed.
example_textbook: If 'it's natural so it's good' justified eating organic food, it would also justify diseases, which are natural too.
example_conversational: If 'we've always done it this way' justifies keeping this process, it'd also justify never updating any tool we use.

name: Psychologist's Fallacy
definition: An observer assumes their own perspective is objective when interpreting someone else's behavior.
pattern: I interpret behavior B as meaning M; therefore B objectively means M.
example_textbook: A therapist assumes a patient's silence means resistance, without considering other explanations.
example_conversational: He didn't respond right away, so obviously he's avoiding the question.

name: Reification
definition: Treating an abstract concept or hypothetical construct as if it were a concrete, real entity with agency.
pattern: Abstract concept C is described as acting/choosing/wanting, as if C were a physical agent.
example_textbook: Evolution 'decides' which traits survive.
example_conversational: The market 'wants' to correct itself, so we should just let it.

name: Retrospective Determinism
definition: Believing that because an event occurred under certain circumstances, those circumstances made the event inevitable.
pattern: Circumstance C preceded event E; therefore C made E inevitable.
example_textbook: He won the lottery while wearing his lucky socks, so the socks made winning inevitable.
example_conversational: We launched on a Tuesday and it went viral, so Tuesday launches are clearly the move.

name: Slippery Slope
definition: Asserting that a small first step will inevitably lead to a chain of events ending in a significant negative outcome, without justifying the chain.
pattern: If A happens, then B, then C... then catastrophe Z; therefore A must not happen.
example_textbook: If we allow students to retake one exam, soon no one will ever take exams seriously again.
example_conversational: If we let people work from home one day a week, next thing you know nobody comes into the office at all.

name: Special Pleading
definition: Claiming an exemption to a generally accepted rule without adequately justifying why the exemption applies.
pattern: Rule R applies generally; X claims to be exempt from R, without sufficient justification.
example_textbook: Everyone should follow the deadline policy, except me, because my situation is different (unexplained).
example_conversational: Late work isn't accepted from anyone else, but in my case it should be, because... it's me.

name: Begging the Question
definition: Using the conclusion of an argument, or an assumption equivalent to it, as one of its own premises.
pattern: X is true because Y, where Y presupposes X.
example_textbook: Smoking is deadly because cigarettes can kill you, and anything that kills is deadly (defines 'deadly' into the premise).
example_conversational: Of course the policy is fair — it's fair because it treats everyone the same way, which is what fairness means, which is why it's fair.

name: Circular Reasoning
definition: An argument whose conclusion is restated as, or directly depends on, one of its own premises.
pattern: X is true because Y; Y is true because X.
example_textbook: The Bible is true because it's the word of God, and we know it's the word of God because the Bible says so.
example_conversational: He's guilty because he failed the test, and the test is accurate because guilty people fail it.

name: Loaded Label
definition: Using an evocative or connotation-laden term to sway a conclusion without directly arguing for it, a form of begging the question.
pattern: Describe X using term T (loaded with approval/disapproval) to imply a conclusion about X.
example_textbook: Organic food is 'safe and healthy,' implying non-organic food is unsafe and unhealthy.
example_conversational: Our plan is the 'common sense' approach, implying any other plan is nonsensical.

name: Fallacy of Many Questions
definition: Asking a question that presupposes something unproven or unaccepted, limiting any direct answer to serve the questioner's agenda.
pattern: Question Q presupposes unproven claim P; any direct answer to Q implicitly affirms P.
example_textbook: Have you stopped cheating on your taxes?
example_conversational: So when did you start ignoring my emails?

name: Accident
definition: Applying a general rule to a specific case where an exception clearly should apply.
pattern: General rule R applies to most cases; case C is an exception; rule R is still applied to C.
example_textbook: Cutting people with knives is illegal; therefore surgeons should be arrested for performing surgery.
example_conversational: Company policy says no exceptions for late arrivals, even though her train was cancelled.

name: No True Scotsman
definition: Making a generalization unfalsifiable by redefining it to exclude any counterexample as it arises.
pattern: All A are B; counterexample C is A but not B; therefore C isn't a 'real' A.
example_textbook: No Scotsman puts sugar on his porridge. But my uncle Angus does. Well, no true Scotsman does.
example_conversational: Real fans never miss a game. But he missed one last week. Well, he's not a real fan then.

name: Cherry Picking
definition: Selecting only the data or cases that support a position while ignoring data that contradicts it.
pattern: Present supporting cases C1, C2, C3; omit contradicting cases C4, C5.
example_textbook: Citing the three studies that support a drug's effectiveness while ignoring the twenty that don't.
example_conversational: He only brings up the quarters where revenue went up, never the ones where it dropped.

name: Nut-Picking
definition: Seeking out fringe, unrepresentative statements from members of an opposing group to portray the whole group as incompetent or irrational.
pattern: Find the most extreme statement from group G; present it as representative of G.
example_textbook: Highlighting one extreme social media comment as representative of an entire political movement.
example_conversational: One guy on the forum said something crazy, so apparently that's what 'everyone in that community' believes.

name: Survivorship Bias
definition: Focusing on the successes of a process while ignoring the (often more numerous) failures, skewing perceived outcomes.
pattern: Successes S1...Sn are visible and promoted; failures are invisible/unmentioned; conclusion drawn from S only.
example_textbook: Studying surviving WWII planes to decide where to add armor, ignoring that planes hit in other places never made it back.
example_conversational: Every successful founder I follow dropped out of college, so dropping out must be the key to success.

name: False Analogy
definition: Drawing a comparison between two things that are not sufficiently similar in the relevant respects.
pattern: A is like B in respect R1; B has property P; therefore A has property P (R1 insufficient to support P).
example_textbook: A company is like a family, so employees should never be let go.
example_conversational: Running a household budget is just like running a national economy, so the government should never run a deficit.

name: Hasty Generalization
definition: Drawing a broad conclusion from a sample that is too small or unrepresentative.
pattern: Sample S (small/unrepresentative) has property P; therefore the whole population has property P.
example_textbook: I met two rude tourists from that country, so people from there must be rude.
example_conversational: Both candidates I interviewed from that school were unprepared, so that program must not teach well.

name: Argument from Anecdote
definition: Using a personal story or isolated example as if it were sufficient evidence for a general claim.
pattern: I/someone experienced X; therefore X is generally true.
example_textbook: My grandfather smoked his whole life and lived to 95, so smoking isn't that dangerous.
example_conversational: My friend took that supplement and felt amazing, so it obviously works.

name: Misleading Vividness
definition: Describing an event in vivid, emotionally striking detail to make it seem more statistically significant than it is.
pattern: Vivid anecdote A described in detail; A treated as more probable/important than base rates suggest.
example_textbook: After hearing one graphic story about a plane crash, refusing to fly despite air travel's overall safety.
example_conversational: After that one horror story about the surgery going wrong, she decided the whole procedure was too risky.

name: Overwhelming Exception
definition: A generalization technically holds but comes with so many qualifications that little of the original claim remains.
pattern: All A are B, except in cases C1, C2, C3... (which cover most actual instances).
example_textbook: Everyone has an equal chance to succeed — except for income, location, education, and connections, which determine most outcomes.
example_conversational: The policy applies to everyone — well, except contractors, except remote staff, except anyone hired before 2020...

name: Cum Hoc Ergo Propter Hoc
definition: Assuming that because two variables are correlated, one must cause the other.
pattern: A correlates with B; therefore A causes B.
example_textbook: Ice cream sales and drowning deaths both rise in summer, so ice cream causes drowning.
example_conversational: Every time we run ads on Fridays, sales go up — the ads must be working (ignoring weekend shopping patterns).

name: Post Hoc Ergo Propter Hoc
definition: Assuming that because X happened before Y, X must have caused Y.
pattern: X occurred; then Y occurred; therefore X caused Y.
example_textbook: I wore my lucky hat and we won the game, so the hat caused the win.
example_conversational: We switched vendors in March and revenue dipped in April, so the new vendor must be the problem.

name: Wrong Direction
definition: Reversing cause and effect, claiming the actual effect is the cause and vice versa.
pattern: A causes B (claimed), when in reality B causes A.
example_textbook: Claiming that carrying lighters causes smoking, when really smokers are the ones who carry lighters.
example_conversational: He says success made him confident, but actually his confidence is what helped him become successful.

name: Ignoring a Common Cause
definition: Concluding A causes B, or vice versa, while ignoring a third factor C that actually causes both.
pattern: A and B are correlated; concluded A causes B; in reality, C causes both A and B.
example_textbook: Concluding that having a lighter causes lung disease, ignoring that smoking causes both.
example_conversational: Teams with more meetings ship slower, so meetings must be the problem — ignoring that complex projects cause both more meetings and slower shipping.

name: Fallacy of the Single Cause
definition: Assuming a single, simple cause for an outcome that actually resulted from multiple contributing causes.
pattern: Outcome O occurred; cause C1 is identified; conclusion: C1 alone caused O (ignoring C2, C3...).
example_textbook: The company failed because of one bad CEO decision, ignoring market conditions, competition, and internal structural issues.
example_conversational: The project failed because the deadline was too tight — never mind the unclear requirements and turnover.

name: Furtive Fallacy
definition: Assuming that significant outcomes must result from the deliberate malfeasance of decision-makers.
pattern: Bad outcome O occurred; therefore someone must have deliberately and secretly caused O.
example_textbook: Assuming a stock market crash must be the result of a deliberate conspiracy rather than emergent systemic factors.
example_conversational: The product launch flopped — someone on the team must have sabotaged it on purpose.

name: Magical Thinking
definition: Believing that one's thoughts, rituals, or symbolic actions can directly cause unrelated real-world outcomes.
pattern: Performing ritual/thought R; therefore unrelated outcome O is more likely.
example_textbook: Knocking on wood to prevent bad luck.
example_conversational: If I just visualize the deal closing hard enough, it'll happen.

name: Observational Interpretation Fallacy
definition: Misinterpreting an association found in an observational study as evidence of a causal relationship.
pattern: Observational study finds A associated with B; concluded A causes B.
example_textbook: An observational study finds coffee drinkers live longer, so coffee is concluded to extend life.
example_conversational: The survey shows employees who use the new tool report higher satisfaction, so the tool must be causing the satisfaction.

name: Regression Fallacy
definition: Ascribing a cause to a change that is actually just natural statistical fluctuation (regression to the mean).
pattern: Extreme value V occurred; intervention I applied; value returns to normal; concluded I caused the return to normal.
example_textbook: A struggling athlete gets a new coach, performance improves (regressing to their normal average), and the coach is credited.
example_conversational: Sales were unusually low last month, we did an emergency promo, and sales bounced back — the promo must have worked.

name: Gambler's Fallacy
definition: The mistaken belief that past independent random outcomes affect the probability of future independent outcomes.
pattern: Random event E has occurred N times in a row; therefore the opposite outcome is 'due' next.
example_textbook: The roulette wheel landed on red 10 times in a row, so black is due next.
example_conversational: We've lost the last three pitches, so we're bound to win the next one.

name: Inverse Gambler's Fallacy
definition: Inferring from an unlikely outcome that the underlying random process must have run many times before.
pattern: Unlikely outcome O observed; therefore the process generating O must have occurred many times.
example_textbook: Seeing someone roll double sixes and assuming they must have been rolling dice for a long time before you arrived.
example_conversational: This algorithm found such a perfect match, it must have run through thousands of attempts behind the scenes.

name: P-Hacking
definition: Believing in the significance of a statistical result without accounting for the number of comparisons or experiments run, only the significant ones being reported.
pattern: Many comparisons run; only the significant result reported; treated as if it were the only test performed.
example_textbook: Testing 20 unrelated correlations and publishing only the one that was statistically significant by chance.
example_conversational: We tried a dozen subject lines and this one had the best open rate, so clearly this exact wording is what works.

name: Garden of Forking Paths Fallacy
definition: Incorrectly believing that a single experiment is immune to the multiple-comparisons problem because only one test was nominally run.
pattern: One experiment run with many possible analysis choices; result treated as if no multiple-comparisons risk existed.
example_textbook: Analyzing one dataset multiple ways until a significant pattern emerges, then reporting it as a single planned test.
example_conversational: We only ran the analysis once — we just looked at it from a few different angles until something popped.

name: Texas Sharpshooter Fallacy
definition: Improperly asserting a cause to explain a cluster of data after the fact, ignoring that clusters can occur randomly.
pattern: Data shows a cluster C; a cause is retroactively proposed to explain C, without prior prediction.
example_textbook: Noticing a cluster of cancer cases in one neighborhood and assuming a specific local cause, without statistical testing.
example_conversational: Three of our best hires all went to the same college, so that college must be where we should focus recruiting.

name: Sunk Costs Fallacy
definition: Continuing a course of action because of the time, money, or effort already invested, rather than its future value.
pattern: Invested resources R in X already; therefore continue with X (regardless of X's future prospects).
example_textbook: Continuing to watch a bad movie because you already paid for the ticket.
example_conversational: We've already spent eight months on this feature, so we have to ship it even though no one wants it anymore.

name: Appeal to the Stone
definition: Dismissing a claim as absurd without providing any proof or argument for why it is absurd.
pattern: X is absurd (asserted, not argued).
example_textbook: Responding to a philosophical argument by simply kicking a stone and saying 'I refute it thus.'
example_conversational: That's ridiculous, I'm not even going to respond to that.

name: Invincible Ignorance
definition: Refusing to accept an argument or evidence, no matter how strong, simply by continuing to disbelieve.
pattern: Present evidence E for X; responder rejects X regardless of E, repeatedly.
example_textbook: No amount of fossil evidence will convince a strict young-earth advocate that the earth is billions of years old.
example_conversational: I don't care what the data says, I just don't believe it, and nothing will change that.

name: Argument from Ignorance
definition: Assuming a claim is true because it hasn't been proven false, or false because it hasn't been proven true.
pattern: X has not been proven false; therefore X is true.
example_textbook: No one has proven aliens don't exist, so they must exist.
example_conversational: You can't prove he didn't do it, so he probably did.

name: Argument from Repetition
definition: Repeating an argument until objections cease, then treating the lack of continued objection as evidence of truth.
pattern: Restate X repeatedly; opposition eventually stops objecting; treat silence as agreement/proof.
example_textbook: Restating a claim in every meeting until people stop pushing back, then citing that as consensus.
example_conversational: I've said this five times now and nobody's arguing anymore, so I guess we all agree.

name: Argument from Silence
definition: Assuming a claim is true (or false) based on the absence of evidence or comment from an authoritative source.
pattern: Source S says nothing about X; therefore X is true/false.
example_textbook: An ancient text doesn't mention a particular event, so historians conclude it never happened.
example_conversational: He never denied the rumor, so it's probably true.

name: Ignoratio Elenchi
definition: Presenting an argument that may be internally valid but fails to address the actual question at issue.
pattern: Argument proves Y; the question at issue was X; Y is irrelevant to X.
example_textbook: Arguing at length that crime is bad in response to a question about whether a specific policy reduces crime.
example_conversational: Asked if the budget overran, he gave a ten-minute answer about how hard the team worked.

name: Red Herring
definition: Introducing an irrelevant topic to divert attention away from the original argument.
pattern: Discussing X; introduce unrelated Y to redirect the conversation away from X.
example_textbook: If you want to complain about the dishes I left in the sink, what about the laundry you never do?
example_conversational: You're asking about the missed deadline, but let's talk about how the client changed requirements three times.

name: Ad Hominem
definition: Attacking the person making an argument rather than addressing the argument itself.
pattern: Person P makes argument A; attack P's character instead of A.
example_textbook: You can't trust his economic plan, he's never even run a business.
example_conversational: Why would we listen to her about the budget, she's always been bad with money personally.

name: Circumstantial Ad Hominem
definition: Dismissing an argument because the arguer benefits from, or is biased toward, its conclusion.
pattern: P argues for X; P benefits from X; therefore X is false.
example_textbook: Of course the tobacco company says cigarettes aren't that harmful — they profit from sales.
example_conversational: Of course he thinks remote work is fine, he wants to keep his home office setup.

name: Poisoning the Well
definition: Presenting adverse information about someone in advance, in order to discredit everything they will subsequently say.
pattern: Before P speaks, present negative info about P; audience discounts everything P says afterward.
example_textbook: Before letting the witness testify, the lawyer mentions her past criminal record to bias the jury.
example_conversational: Before you hear his side, you should know he's lied to me before.

name: Appeal to Motive
definition: Dismissing an idea by questioning the motives of the person proposing it, rather than its substance.
pattern: P proposes X; P's motive for proposing X is questioned; therefore X is dismissed.
example_textbook: She only supports the new policy because it benefits her department.
example_conversational: He's just saying that because he wants credit for the idea.

name: Tone Policing
definition: Focusing on the emotional tone of a message rather than its content, to discredit or dismiss it.
pattern: P makes claim C with emotional tone T; responder objects to T instead of addressing C.
example_textbook: I might agree with you if you weren't so angry about it.
example_conversational: You'd have a better point if you didn't sound so frustrated right now.

name: Traitorous Critic Fallacy
definition: Portraying a critic's perceived affiliation as the real reason for their criticism, and demanding they recuse themselves entirely.
pattern: Critic C (affiliated with group G) criticizes X; response: C should have no say because of G.
example_textbook: You used to work there, so your criticism of the company doesn't count.
example_conversational: You're not even on this team anymore, why are you weighing in on how we run sprints?

name: Bulverism
definition: Assuming an argument is wrong by speculating about the psychological reason someone holds it, without addressing the argument.
pattern: P argues X; explain why P psychologically believes X; conclude X is false.
example_textbook: You only think that because you're insecure about your own choices.
example_conversational: You're just saying that because you're stressed about the deadline.

name: Appeal to Authority
definition: Treating a claim as true solely because an authority figure asserts it, even outside their area of expertise or against the evidence.
pattern: Authority A says X; therefore X is true (regardless of evidence or relevance of A's expertise).
example_textbook: A famous physicist says a particular diet is healthy, so it must be true.
example_conversational: Our CEO said this approach will work, and he's been right before, so it'll work.

name: Appeal to Accomplishment
definition: Judging a claim as true or false based on the accomplishments (or lack thereof) of the person making it.
pattern: P has accomplishment A; therefore P's claim X is true (regardless of evidence for X).
example_textbook: She built a billion-dollar company, so her opinion on parenting must be correct.
example_conversational: He's published twenty papers, so obviously his take on this unrelated topic is right too.

name: Courtier's Reply
definition: Dismissing a critic by claiming they lack the credentials or deep knowledge required to comment, rather than engaging the criticism.
pattern: Critic C criticizes X; response: C hasn't studied X deeply enough to have an opinion.
example_textbook: You haven't read all the theological texts, so your criticism of religion is invalid.
example_conversational: You haven't actually used the framework in production, so your critique of it doesn't count.

name: Appeal to Consequences
definition: Arguing that a claim must be true or false based on whether its consequences are desirable or undesirable.
pattern: If X is true, consequence C (bad) follows; therefore X is false.
example_textbook: Free will can't be an illusion, because if it were, no one could be held morally responsible.
example_conversational: It can't be true that the project is behind schedule, because then we'd have to tell the client bad news.

name: Appeal to Emotion
definition: Manipulating an audience's emotions in place of presenting valid reasoning.
pattern: Evoke emotional response E; use E to obtain agreement with X (without evidence for X).
example_textbook: Think of the children — how could you possibly oppose this law?
example_conversational: After everything this team has sacrificed, how could you even consider cutting the budget?

name: Appeal to Fear
definition: Generating fear, anxiety, or distress in the audience to obtain agreement, rather than presenting evidence.
pattern: If not X, then terrible outcome O; therefore X.
example_textbook: If we don't pass this law, crime will spiral out of control.
example_conversational: If we don't approve this budget right now, the whole project could collapse.

name: Appeal to Flattery
definition: Using excessive or insincere praise to win agreement rather than relying on evidence.
pattern: Praise audience/listener; therefore listener should agree with speaker's claim.
example_textbook: Someone as smart as you can clearly see why this plan is the right one.
example_conversational: You're way too sharp to fall for the other team's pitch — you'll see ours is the better choice.

name: Appeal to Pity
definition: Generating sympathy or mercy in the listener as a substitute for actual evidence or justification.
pattern: P is in a sympathetic situation; therefore P's claim/request should be granted.
example_textbook: I should pass this class — my whole semester has been so hard, with family issues and everything.
example_conversational: I know I missed the deadline, but it's been such a rough month, you have to understand.

name: Appeal to Ridicule
definition: Mocking or portraying an opponent's position as laughable rather than addressing its substance.
pattern: Position X is presented as absurd/ridiculous (mockingly), without addressing its merits.
example_textbook: Oh sure, and next you'll tell me the moon is made of cheese.
example_conversational: Right, because that plan is just going to magically fix everything, sure.

name: Appeal to Spite
definition: Generating bitterness or hostility toward an opponent to win agreement, rather than presenting evidence.
pattern: Evoke resentment toward opponent O; use that resentment to support a conclusion against O's position.
example_textbook: After everything they've done to us, how could you possibly side with them on this?
example_conversational: You really want to agree with the guy who threw you under the bus last quarter?

name: Pooh-Pooh
definition: Dismissing an opponent's argument as unworthy of consideration, typically through derisive language, rather than refuting it.
pattern: Dismiss X as silly/unserious (without rebuttal).
example_textbook: That theory isn't even worth discussing.
example_conversational: Yeah, that idea's not really worth our time.

name: Style Over Substance
definition: Judging an argument's validity by the eloquence or aesthetic appeal of its delivery rather than its content.
pattern: X is stated eloquently/memorably; therefore X is judged more true or persuasive.
example_textbook: An ill caused is well excused (rhyming makes the claim feel more credible than it is).
example_conversational: He delivered that pitch so smoothly, it must be a solid plan.

name: Wishful Thinking
definition: Believing or arguing for something because it would be pleasant if true, rather than because of evidence.
pattern: X would be pleasant/desirable; therefore X is true.
example_textbook: I just know everything will work out fine, so I'm not going to worry about the numbers.
example_conversational: I really feel like the client will love this without changes, so let's not bother testing it.

name: Appeal to Nature
definition: Judging something as good or bad solely based on whether it is 'natural' or 'unnatural.'
pattern: X is natural; therefore X is good (or X is unnatural; therefore X is bad).
example_textbook: This supplement is all-natural, so it must be safe.
example_conversational: It's a totally organic process, so there's no way it could be harmful.

name: Appeal to Novelty
definition: Claiming a proposal is superior solely because it is new or modern.
pattern: X is new; therefore X is better than older alternatives.
example_textbook: This is the latest management framework, so it must outperform the old one.
example_conversational: It's a brand-new tool, so it's bound to be better than what we're using now.

name: Appeal to Poverty
definition: Supporting a conclusion because the arguer is poor, or rejecting it because the arguer is wealthy.
pattern: P is poor; therefore P's claim X is true.
example_textbook: He's struggled financially his whole life, so his investment advice must be trustworthy.
example_conversational: She grew up with nothing, so she clearly knows the right way to manage money.

name: Appeal to Tradition
definition: Supporting a conclusion solely because it has long been believed or practiced.
pattern: X has always been done/believed; therefore X is correct.
example_textbook: We've always done performance reviews this way, so it must be the right approach.
example_conversational: This is how my parents raised me, so it's clearly the right way to raise kids.

name: Appeal to Wealth
definition: Supporting a conclusion because the arguer is wealthy, or rejecting it because the arguer is poor.
pattern: P is wealthy; therefore P's claim X is true.
example_textbook: He's a billionaire, so his business advice must be correct.
example_conversational: She's clearly successful, so whatever strategy she's using must be the right one.

name: Argumentum ad Baculum
definition: Supporting a position through threats or coercion rather than evidence.
pattern: Accept X, or face threat T; therefore accept X.
example_textbook: Agree with the policy, or you'll be looking for a new job.
example_conversational: You'd better agree this was the right call, if you know what's good for your career here.

name: Argumentum ad Populum
definition: Claiming a proposition is true or good solely because many or most people believe it.
pattern: Most people believe X; therefore X is true.
example_textbook: Everyone is investing in this, so it must be a good investment.
example_conversational: Literally every other team has switched to this tool, so we should too.

name: Association Fallacy
definition: Arguing that because two things share, or are implied to share, a property, they must be the same or equally good/bad.
pattern: A is associated with B; B has property P; therefore A has property P.
example_textbook: He supports the same policy as a disgraced politician, so his motives must be just as corrupt.
example_conversational: That vendor also works with a company we had problems with, so they're probably trouble too.

name: Logic Chopping
definition: Focusing on minor, trivial details of an argument while ignoring its main point.
pattern: Argument A makes main point M with minor flaw F; response attacks only F, ignoring M.
example_textbook: Dismissing an entire research paper's conclusion because of a single typo in a footnote.
example_conversational: You said 'about ten people' but it was actually eleven, so I don't think your whole point holds up.

name: Ipse Dixit
definition: Presenting a claim as self-evidently or dogmatically true without any supporting argument.
pattern: X is true (asserted, with no support given).
example_textbook: That's just how it is.
example_conversational: It's obvious that this approach is correct, I don't need to explain why.

name: Chronological Snobbery
definition: Dismissing an idea as incorrect because it was popular at the same time as some other belief now known to be false.
pattern: Belief B was common alongside false belief F (in the same era); therefore B is also false.
example_textbook: People in the past believed in spontaneous generation and also believed in classical logic, so classical logic must be outdated too.
example_conversational: That management style is from the same era as a lot of outdated office culture, so it must not work anymore.

name: Fallacy of Relative Privation
definition: Dismissing a concern or complaint by pointing to a supposedly more important problem elsewhere.
pattern: X is a problem; but Y is a worse problem elsewhere; therefore X doesn't matter.
example_textbook: Why worry about office snacks when there are people starving in the world?
example_conversational: You're upset about a delayed paycheck? People have real problems, you know.

name: Genetic Fallacy
definition: Judging a claim as true or false based solely on its origin, rather than its current merits.
pattern: X originated from source S; therefore X is true/false (based on S alone).
example_textbook: That idea came from a rival company, so it must be a bad idea.
example_conversational: That suggestion came from the intern, so I doubt it's worth considering.

name: I'm Entitled to My Opinion
definition: Deflecting any challenge to a claim by asserting a right to hold the opinion, rather than defending its truth.
pattern: Challenge to claim X; response: I'm entitled to my opinion (avoiding the substance of the challenge).
example_textbook: Well, that's just my opinion and I'm entitled to it.
example_conversational: I can think whatever I want about this, you don't have to agree.

name: Moralistic Fallacy
definition: Inferring factual claims about what is from premises about what ought to be, violating the fact-value distinction.
pattern: X ought to be true; therefore X is true.
example_textbook: People shouldn't be naturally selfish, so human nature must not really be selfish.
example_conversational: Discrimination shouldn't affect outcomes, so it probably doesn't actually affect them much.

name: Naturalistic Fallacy
definition: Inferring evaluative (ought) conclusions purely from factual (is) premises, violating the fact-value distinction.
pattern: X is the case; therefore X ought to be the case.
example_textbook: Aggression occurs in nature, so aggression must be morally acceptable.
example_conversational: This is just how the industry has always operated, so that's how it should keep operating.

name: Straw Man
definition: Misrepresenting an opponent's argument in a weaker or distorted form, then refuting that distorted version instead of the original.
pattern: P argues X; misrepresent X as X' (weaker/distorted); refute X' as if it refuted X.
example_textbook: Person A: We should regulate emissions. Person B: So you want to shut down all factories and destroy the economy?
example_conversational: I said we should review the budget more carefully. You're saying I want to cancel the whole project?

name: Tu Quoque
definition: Dismissing a position by pointing out that its proponent fails to act consistently with it, rather than addressing the position itself.
pattern: P argues X is wrong; P has also done X; therefore X is not actually wrong / P's argument is invalid.
example_textbook: You say smoking is bad, but you used to smoke yourself!
example_conversational: You're telling me to be on time, but you showed up late to the last three meetings.

name: Two Wrongs Make a Right
definition: Assuming that committing a second wrong act somehow cancels out or justifies the first.
pattern: Wrong act A was done to P; therefore P doing wrong act B in response is justified.
example_textbook: They lied to us first, so it's fine that we lied to them.
example_conversational: They missed our deadline once, so it's only fair we miss theirs.

name: Vacuous Truth
definition: Making a claim that is technically true but meaningless because the relevant category it refers to is empty.
pattern: No A in B has property C, stated when there are no A in B at all.
example_textbook: None of the unicorns in my garden are purple (true, because there are no unicorns at all).
example_conversational: None of our remote employees have complained about the office coffee (we have zero remote employees).

name: Naturalistic Fallacy Fallacy
definition: Incorrectly inferring, from the general invalidity of the is-ought fallacy, that no factual premise can ever support any evaluative conclusion.
pattern: Is-ought inferences are generally invalid; therefore no is-statement can ever justify any ought-statement.
example_textbook: Claiming that facts about suffering can never have any bearing on whether causing suffering is wrong.
example_conversational: You can't use any data about harm to argue this policy is wrong — that's just an is-ought fallacy, full stop.
